analysis.one_liner: Makes state consumer protection and anti-predatory-lending laws apply to national banks and federal thrifts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after referral in July 2005 it sat in a House Financial Services subcommittee and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended a recent regulatory practice of shielding national banks and federal savings associations from state consumer protection laws. It would have let state rules on unfair lending, foreclosure, repossession, collections, and high-cost "predatory" mortgages apply to those banks, sharply limited the federal banking regulators' power to wipe state laws off the books, and given state attorneys general explicit authority to sue national banks on behalf of their residents. It would also have required the regulators to log every consumer complaint and report them to Congress twice a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers, especially mortgage borrowers in states with strong consumer and anti-predatory-lending laws, and the state attorneys general who would regain the ability to enforce those laws and recover damages for residents against national banks and federal thrifts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers and state attorneys general

how_it_helps.text: Any consumer protection in state law of general application — including unfair or deceptive practices laws, consumer fraud laws, and repossession, foreclosure, and collection rules — would apply to national banks and federal savings associations [S2, S3].

State laws offering stronger protection against high-cost, predatory mortgage loans than federal Truth in Lending rules would apply to national banks and federal thrifts, closing the gap that let federally chartered lenders avoid state anti-predatory-lending laws [S2, S3].

The Comptroller of the Currency and the Director of the Office of Thrift Supervision could preempt a state law only when a comparable federal statute or regulation expressly governs the same activity — a much narrower standard than the regulators were asserting at the time [S2, S3].

State attorneys general would be expressly authorized to bring actions to enforce federal or state law against national banks and federal thrifts and to seek relief and damages on behalf of state residents, and private parties could enforce their rights in court even when a federal regulator brings its own enforcement action [S2, S3].

Both regulators would have to record and monitor every consumer complaint and resolution, and post semiannual reports to Congress on their consumer protection work, including complaint counts by state law, on their websites [S2, S3].

State consumer laws would also keep applying to state-chartered nondepository subsidiaries, affiliates, and agents of national banks and federal thrifts, so a company could not shield itself by placing a unit under a federally chartered bank [S3].

analysis.who_pays: National banks and federal savings associations, which would lose the regulatory shield that had exempted them from state consumer laws and would face state lawsuits, private claims, and the cost of complying with rules that vary by state — costs that could be passed to customers through fees and rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves the banks' federal power to set interest rates free of state limits: its preemption standard applies to consumer credit and deposit regulation "except in relation to interest pursuant to section 5197," so state usury caps would still not reach national-bank credit cards or loans [S3].

Banks and federal regulators argued in this period that a single national rulebook is safer and cheaper than fifty state standards, and that state enforcement of federally chartered banks duplicates federal supervision and invites inconsistent demands — a real cost the bill's supporters had to weigh.

Applying varied state laws to banks operating nationwide would raise compliance costs, some of which could be passed on to customers, and the bill offers no mechanism to harmonize conflicting state requirements beyond barring state laws that discriminate against national banks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the core trade was straightforward: state anti-predatory-lending and fraud laws would reach the largest lenders, at the price of a patchier rulebook and possible higher compliance costs. The bill's biggest honest weakness is what it left out — banks would keep their federal interest-rate advantage, so state usury limits still would not apply to national-bank credit cards. As a consumer-protection measure, though, the benefits to borrowers facing predatory loans were concrete and the costs largely fell on the industry.

outcome.mechanism: After being referred to the Financial Services Committee and then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, the bill sat there and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on July 26, 2005, joined at introduction by Representatives Barney Frank of Massachusetts, Barbara Lee, and Carolyn McCarthy, and it drew 11 cosponsors — 9 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S1, S3, S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 24, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and that was the last action the bill ever received [S5].

The bill's timing put it directly against a policy the federal banking regulator had adopted in 2004 asserting broad power to override state consumer laws for national banks; the bill would have reversed that by statute, but no committee or floor vote ever took place [S2, S3].
The Republican-led Financial Services Committee never scheduled a markup or floor action, and the bill expired with the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National banks, federal savings associations, and mortgage lenders came out ahead: the regulatory shield that kept state consumer protection and anti-predatory-lending laws out of their operations stayed in place because the bill died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's 11 cosponsors included 9 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican, while the Republican chairman of the Financial Services Committee never moved it toward a vote.

industries.industry: National banks and federal savings associations
industries.note: The bill would strip their federal shield from state consumer protection, fraud, foreclosure, and anti-predatory-lending laws, exposing them to state attorney general suits and private claims. That shield had kept many customer complaints out of state courts, so its loss is the bill's main cost to the industry and main gain for consumers.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders, including nondepository affiliates of national banks
industries.note: State laws against high-cost and predatory mortgage loans would apply to federally chartered lenders, and the bill expressly keeps state law reaching their nondepository subsidiaries and agents, preventing an end-run around state lending rules.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and state consumer enforcement
industries.note: The bill explicitly authorizes chief state law enforcement officers to sue national banks and federal thrifts on behalf of residents and recover damages, restoring an enforcement channel that federal preemption had narrowed.

industries.industry: National bank credit card and consumer lending pricing
industries.note: Even this bill leaves intact the federal rule letting national banks charge interest under whichever state's rates they choose, so state usury caps still would not apply to their credit cards — the one area where the industry's federal advantage survives.
